summary: A local feature traces the city's transit and traffic history from post-WWII bus and subway beginnings, through the late-1980s boom, to the congestion of September 2023. It covers voices from officials, activists and business leaders, and debates over BRT, cycle lanes and congestion charging. It closes with current efforts such as Velocity Innovations' smart signal pilots and the refurbished Metro Line 2.
one_line: A narrative on how the city's transit system grew, fell behind rising car traffic, and is now seeking fixes like smart signals and Metro Line 2's refurbishment.
key_facts: Traffic congestion has grown increasingly severe in the city since the beginning of September 2023.
The transit system began in the decades after the Second World War, with the first bus lines overseen by transit pioneer Edward J. Roberts.
The first subway outlets were mapped out by engineer Carol S. Thompson.
Longtime resident Jameson Kirkwood recalls a time when 'the patter of the bus approaching was pretty much the only sound on otherwise peaceful mid-morning streets.'
The economic boom of the late 1980s brought more people and cars, turning sleepy neighbourhoods into congested ones.
Business mogul Rachel Aniston's corporation set down roots in 1991; she says they did not grasp the strain growth would place on the streets.
By September 2023, every arterial route into downtown was congested, with commuters stuck bumper to bumper.
Environmental consultant Maya Enriquez says the problem includes pollution, stress and inefficiency, and calls for 'a paradigm shift.'
Transport Commissioner Aiden Winters admits the city has been 'playing catch-up, responding to problems instead of anticipating them.'
Measures debated include Bus Rapid Transit (BRT) systems, expanded cycle lanes, and congestion charging for city centers.
Local activist Lila Greenway pushes for environmentally friendly options, urging incentives for public transport and safer walking and cycling.
The city is collaborating with tech giant Velocity Innovations on pilot projects for smart signal systems.
Dr. Nora El-Masry of Velocity Innovations says smart signals can decrease traffic congestion by up to 40%.
The old Metro Line 2 has been refurbished and is celebrated as a revival of a venerable city icon.
Obstacles to progress include fiscal constraints and policy deadlocks.
